units: a woman speaking for a residents' group sets out their demands
she sorts these demands into three themes
the first theme concerns street lights that stop working at night
the second theme bears on rubbish left on the ground
the third theme targets the danger of a junction that is too narrow
an occupant of a neighbouring dwelling reports a building-site hoarding that blocks the view
a public official announces that a survey has begun
a meeting open to the public is promised for soon
every household that signed will receive a letter in reply
text: Speaking for the residents' group, the woman chosen to put their case sorted the complaints under three headings. Lighting came first. Every other lamp along the lane beside the old works, she said, goes dark once night falls. Cleanliness came second: cigarette ends piling up under the benches, and bags dumped well clear of the bins meant for them. The junction came third, where bicycles and delivery vans squeeze onto a road built for far less. A tenant from the corner block added that the hoarding round the neighbouring site blocks the view from the pavement. The official handling the matter replied that a survey is already under way, and that a meeting open to everyone would be held before the season is out. Every household that signed the register, he promised, would get a written answer.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the earliest communities gathered near a source of water
that spot gave rise to the notion of common ground
a well was first sunk and then ringed with a rim
a stone seat there took in the oldest among them
collective affairs were talked over beside the well
the spread of settlements brought arcades around the open ground
trade came to be added to public speech
a roofed building then sheltered the traders from bad weather
the place served for publishing and for contesting common decisions
text: Long before streets carried names on plates, people gathered where the water was, and out of that habit grew the idea of ground belonging to everyone. A well was sunk first; a rim of stone was raised around it, and then a low bench where the oldest of the settlement sat. It became usual to talk beside that well about whatever concerned the whole group. As the settlements spread, arcades were built along the edges of the open ground, and goods began to change hands where words had changed hands before. Later a roofed hall went up, its pillars keeping the stalls dry through wet evenings. The square ended up as the place where common decisions were read out, listened to, and shouted down when they displeased. That slow layering explains the fondness so many still feel for an empty space hemmed in by walls.

units: the tiredness caused by night-time noise depends above all on the shape of the surrounding walls
hard surfaces send sound back instead of soaking it up
a shout in an enclosed courtyard returns as an echo to whoever is asleep
an abrupt change in level interrupts deep sleep
the sleeper may wake without keeping any memory of it
exhaustion lowers the capacity to put up with noise
heightened annoyance leads on to complaints
designers use absorbent materials and planting
a soft surface takes energy out of the sound wave
text: What wears you down in night-time noise has less to do with how loud it is than with the shape of the walls around the bed. Smooth render and glass throw sound back instead of soaking it up, so a raised voice in an enclosed courtyard returns as an echo to the ear of whoever is asleep. Deep sleep breaks at the smallest jump in level, which is why a sleeper surfaces again and again with no memory of having done so. Then the effect compounds. Tiredness lowers what a person will put up with; a lowered threshold turns ordinary noise into a nuisance; the nuisance ends in a complaint. Planners answer with open-pored materials, hedges set along the fences, and surfaces that damp the rumble of wheels. Every soft face takes a share of energy out of the wave, and a weakened wave no longer crosses the walls.

units: a dispute arises from a bin left open in a shared courtyard
the residents of one block blame the others for leaving bags on the ground
the latter answer that the passage is blocked by bicycles
the written exchanges turn hostile
two households break off all contact
a woman employed in the building suggests drawing a sketch of the courtyard together
each participant was to mark their routes and their drop-off points
the sketch shows that a blocked-up doorway forced every route through the same point
reopening that doorway and a low fence put an end to the quarrel
text: The whole thing started with a complaint about a bin that had been left standing open in the shared courtyard of a housing estate. Households on the north side accused those on the south of dropping their bags on the ground; the south side answered that the north side filled the passage with bicycles. Letters grew curt, tempers followed, and two families stopped speaking altogether. The caretaker then put forward an odd suggestion: bring both sides together, not to argue, but to draw the courtyard. Everyone was to mark where they set things down and which way they walked. What the drawing showed was a blocked-up doorway that funnelled every route through a single corner. The doorway was opened again, a low fence divided the ground, and the complaint was withdrawn before anything formal came of it.

units: two methods exist for consulting the residents of a block
the first sets up a voting arrangement in the entrance for a week
a voting slip is delivered to each letterbox
the count takes an evening and two observers
the presence of observers heads off objections to the outcome
the second method uses an accessible book in which each person writes and signs
the confidential ballot keeps opinions private
the open book makes the reasoning visible and shifts positions
the secret ballot is chosen for questions that set residents against one another
text: There are two ways for a residents' committee to find out what the occupants of a block really think, and they do not serve the same ends. The first is to stand a ballot box in the entrance hall for a week, with a voting slip posted through every letterbox. Allow an evening for the count, and arrange for two witnesses, so that nobody can pick the outcome apart afterwards. The second replaces the box with an open book, left on a table by the stairs, in which each person writes an opinion and signs it. A closed vote keeps views private and suits touchy subjects; the open book puts the reasoning on show, and opinions often shift because of it. Go for the box when the question sets households against one another, and for the book when the point is to think something through together.

units: a covered market is described through its different phases
the setting up of the stalls happens very early
the sellers squabble then over the empty wooden pallets
the period of heavy footfall makes the aisles very narrow
parents with a pushchair give up the visit and leave by the back
the packing away in the evening is reckoned the hardest
it obliges them to pack up the unsold goods
the traders help one another by lending equipment
one of them keeps an eye on the stall of a colleague who is away
text: Push through the swing doors of the market hall and the first thing you hear is the clatter of trolleys. The place runs on three rhythms, and the traders will tell you so without being asked. There is the setting up, before dawn, when each of them raises a stall and squabbles over the empty pallets. There is the thick of the crowd, when the aisles close in so tightly that pushchairs give up and turn back through the rear doors. And there is the pulling down at night, the worst of the three, the one nobody cares to talk about, because the unsold boxes have to be packed away again. Between the three runs a quieter life: a set of scales lent across the aisle, an eye kept on the stall of whoever has gone off to eat. One seller sums it up, laughing: they bicker endlessly, and they never let each other down.

units: the cleaning staff take over the space at sunrise
they gather up the leaves that fell during the night
delivery people and then office staff arrive after them
those staff cross the place without paying it any attention
a noisy procession of cyclists cuts the space in two
the public seats fill up in the early afternoon
a water basin has been out of service since the cold season
its rim serves as a rest for setting bags down
late in the evening the premises put their chairs outside
text: At first light the square belongs to the sweepers, who push the night's fallen leaves ahead of them along the paving. The delivery men come a little later, and after them the staff from the offices round about, cutting across on the diagonal without once looking up. A column of cyclists splits the space down the middle, horns and whistles together, and vanishes down the lower avenue. By early afternoon the benches have filled: older people, teenagers perched on the backrests, a mother keeping an eye on a pram. The fountain in the middle has stood dry since the cold weather came, and its rim now does duty as a shelf for shopping. As the sun drops behind the roofs the square changes colour and changes company: chairs come out onto the pavement, windows light up one by one, and the stone still gives back the warmth it took in.

units: public seats have been removed in front of a building
the place is now deserted
that emptying follows directly from the removal of the seats
the removal answered late-night gatherings and litter
a lingering smell was invoked as well
the seats also benefited peaceable users
an elderly woman used to break her walk there
the lack of anything to sit on removes the usual presence of passers-by
the presence of seated people made the place safe
text: The benches were taken off the forecourt, and now we profess surprise that nobody stops there. That is not chance; it follows. The case for removing them began with a genuine nuisance: gatherings that ran late, empty bottles, a smell that clung under the arcades. Take away the seat and you take away the gathering, and so far the arithmetic held. But the seat served more than the people who caused trouble. It served the old woman who breaks her walk in two, the delivery man catching his breath, the boy waiting for a friend. With nothing to sit on, those people no longer pause, and the space empties of its ordinary witnesses. Yet it was the gaze of seated passers-by that made the forecourt safe. In driving out the use we disliked, we drove out the quiet watch that held it in check.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a professional carries out mediation in a very crowded district
she takes on quarrels that the courts will not look into
most complaints concern noise rubbish and parking
punishment worsens tensions without changing habits
she begins by listing the complaints block by block
she spots the places where people's comings and goings disturb the rest of others
she holds short meetings given over to a single matter
the undertakings given are written down
a check takes place about six weeks later
text: Her work is mediation in a district where people live packed close, and the quarrels that reach her are the ones neither the police nor the courts will take on. The difficulty is one of numbers. Most of what gets reported comes down to noise, bins and parking, and none of the three yields to punishment, which hardens both sides while leaving the habit untouched. So she works in steps that can be measured. She lists the complaints block by block, then marks the places where one household's coming and going runs into another's rest. After that she calls short meetings, each about a single matter, and writes down whatever is undertaken. A check follows six weeks on. Of the files reopened after that check, she says, the share is a very small part of what she handles in a year.

units: two reworkings of nearby spaces are set side by side
the first concerns a school yard given a cushioned surface
that place also has planters and tiered seating
the children spread themselves unevenly across it
each installation imposes a single way of using it
the second scheme takes over derelict ground for a far smaller outlay
its look seems unfinished with low walls left unrendered
a greater variety of activities is observed there
the absence of any imposed use explains that variety
text: Two neighbouring schemes a short walk apart invite comparison, and the verdict is not the one the drawings promised. The first gave the school yard a soft surface, planters and timber tiers; the work is neat, yet the children bunch up in some corners and desert others, because each piece of kit calls for one posture and leaves little room for invention. The second, on derelict ground nearby, cost a good deal less and looks unfinished: rolled earth, low walls left rough, young trees behind a temporary fence. And there you see a range of uses the first never gets, precisely because nothing there tells you what any one surface is meant for. Designers might do well to keep the lesson in mind. The most polished piece of ground is not automatically the one that takes in the richest life.
